chapters.name: Chapter 1: Picking and planning your side hustle

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding an idea that fits you
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick a side hustle idea that fits your skills, time and neighborhood.
This lesson builds toward: Given your skills and the hours you really have, you will choose a safe side hustle idea that fits your schedule and check that people would pay for it, asking at least three people.
The best side hustle uses something you already do well and solves a problem for someone nearby. Good at math? Tutor younger kids. Love animals? Pet sit or walk dogs. Good with video? Edit clips for a local team or church.
Ask AI: "I am 15, I have 5 hours a week, I am good at drawing and video games, and I live near a park. Give me 10 side hustle ideas that are safe for a teen." Then pick ideas that fit your real time and school schedule.
Check that there are people who want it. Ask three neighbors, family friends or classmates: "Would you pay for this?"
Step by step:
- List your skills and the hours you really have.
- Ask AI for 10 safe ideas that match.
- Cross out ideas that do not fit school or your schedule.
- Ask three people if they would pay for your top idea.
Words to know:
- Side hustle: a small way to earn money outside school or a main job.
- Customer: the person who pays for what you offer.
Try it now: Write your skills and the hours you really have each week. Ask AI for 10 safe side hustle ideas, pick your top one, and ask three people if they would pay for it.
You can now choose a side hustle idea that fits you and that people want.

check.q: What makes a strong side hustle idea?
options: The idea that sounds coolest online
It uses a skill you have and solves a problem for someone nearby
The one that needs the most hours
check.why: The best side hustle uses something you already do well and solves a nearby problem.

check.q: You love your idea, but no one you ask would pay for it. What do you do?
options: Keep asking until someone says yes
Try another idea from your list
check.why: Asking people checks demand; if no one would pay, pick another idea.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Rules, safety and your parent or guardian
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check the youth work rules and agree on safety rules with a parent or guardian.
This lesson builds toward: With a parent or guardian, you will check the federal and state youth work rules and the IRS self-employment tax rule, and agree on safety rules, with at least two safety rules you both agree on.
Some work has age rules. Under federal law, casual babysitting and small chores around private homes are not covered by the child labor rules, and work for a business wholly owned by your parents has special rules. Most other jobs need you to be 14 or older, and no one under 18 may do hazardous work. States can have stricter rules, so check your state's labor office.
Money rules: if your net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more in a year, the IRS says you must file and pay self-employment tax, no matter how old you are. Ask a parent or guardian to help you keep records and check irs.gov.
Safety rules matter most: a parent or guardian knows where you are and who you are working for, you meet new customers with an adult, you never go into a stranger's home alone, and you never post your home address online. Many payment apps and selling sites require an adult, so let your parent or guardian handle them.
Step by step:
- Check the federal youth work rules and your state's rules.
- Show your plan to a parent or guardian.
- Agree on safety rules together.
- Let an adult handle payment apps and selling accounts.
Words to know:
- Self-employed: working for yourself instead of for a boss.
- Net earnings: money you made minus what you spent to make it.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Labor Fact Sheet #43: Child labor rules for nonagricultural jobs
- IRS: Self-employment tax (Social Security and Medicare taxes)
Try it now: Look up your state's youth work rules and read the IRS self-employment tax page with a parent or guardian. Write three safety rules you both agree on.
You can now check the rules for your side hustle and set safety rules with a parent or guardian.

check.q: Under federal law, what kind of work may no one under 18 do?
check.why: Federal law bars anyone under 18 from hazardous work.

check.q: A new customer asks you to come alone to their home to meet. What do you do?
options: Meet them with a parent or guardian, who knows where you are
check.why: Meet new customers with an adult and never go into a stranger's home alone.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Setting a fair price
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a price that covers your costs, pays you fairly and fits your customers.
This lesson builds toward: For one service, you will set a fair price that covers your costs and your time and fits local prices, checked with real people, not only AI.
To set a price, look at three things: what it costs you (supplies, travel), what similar teens or local services charge, and how much your time is worth.
Ask AI to help you think, not to decide: "I walk dogs for 30 minutes. Help me think about a fair price for a teen in a small town. What questions should I ask?" Then ask real people what they pay locally, because AI does not know your neighborhood.
Write your price clearly, for example "Dog walk, 30 minutes" with the amount. Keep it simple and the same for everyone.
Step by step:
- Add up your costs per job.
- Ask people what similar services cost locally.
- Decide what your time is worth.
- Write one clear price for each service.
Words to know:
- Cost: what you spend to do the job.
- Profit: money left after you pay your costs.
Try it now: List your costs for one job, ask two people what they pay for something similar, and write one clear price for your service.
You can now set a fair, clear price for your side hustle.

check.q: Which three things help you set a price?
options: Your costs, local prices and what your time is worth
The highest price you can find online
check.why: A fair price covers your costs, fits local prices and pays you for your time.

check.q: AI suggests a price for lawn mowing. What do you do before you use it?
options: Ask real people what they pay locally
check.why: AI does not know your neighborhood, so check local prices with real people.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Making a simple flyer with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write and design a clear flyer for your service.
This lesson builds toward: Using AI and a free design tool, you will create a flyer with a headline, three short points, a price and a call to action, with no home address and a contact your parent or guardian approves.
A flyer tells people what you do, how much it costs and how to reach you. AI can help with the words: "Write a short, friendly flyer for a teen dog-walking service. Include a headline, 3 bullet points and a call to action."
Design it in a free tool like Canva, Google Docs or Google Slides. Use one big headline, short lines and easy-to-read colors.
Safety: never put your home address on a flyer. Use a parent's or guardian's phone number or email, or a contact they approve. Ask before you post flyers on boards in stores, libraries or community centers.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for a headline, 3 bullets and a call to action.
- Edit the words so they sound like you.
- Design it in a free tool.
- Use a contact a parent or guardian approves, never your address.
Words to know:
- Call to action: a line that tells people what to do next, like "Text to book a walk".
- Headline: the big title at the top.
Try it now: Ask AI to write flyer text for your service. Edit it so it sounds like you, design it in a free tool, and add a contact your parent or guardian approves.
You can now make a clear, safe flyer for your side hustle.

check.q: What is the headline on a flyer?
options: The big line at the top that says what you offer
The small print at the bottom
check.why: A flyer uses one big headline so people see what you offer fast.

check.q: Your AI flyer text includes your home street. What do you do?
options: Leave it so people can find you
Remove it and use a contact your parent or guardian approves
check.why: Never put your home address on a flyer; use an approved contact.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Tracking money in and money out
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a simple money tracker and use it for every job.
This lesson builds toward: For every job and purchase, you will track money in and money out in a four-column tracker and calculate your profit, recording each entry the same day and checking it weekly.
Business owners track every dollar. A simple tracker has four columns: date, money in, money out, and notes (who paid, what you bought).
Make it in Google Sheets, Microsoft Excel, or a paper notebook. AI can help: "Make a simple money tracker table for a teen pet-sitting business with a total at the bottom." Never type bank or card numbers into AI.
Look at it every week. Money in minus money out is your profit. Your records also help a parent or guardian with any tax questions.
Step by step:
- Make four columns: date, money in, money out, notes.
- Write every job and every purchase the same day.
- Add a total row.
- Check it weekly: money in minus money out is profit.
Words to know:
- Spreadsheet: a table on a computer, like Google Sheets or Excel.
- Profit: money in minus money out.
Try it now: Make a money tracker with the four columns. Add two pretend or real jobs and one purchase, and work out your profit.
You can now track your side hustle's money and know your profit.

check.q: What goes in the "money out" column?
options: What you spent, such as supplies or travel
check.why: Money out is what you spend; money in is what customers pay you.

check.q: You want AI to help build your tracker. What do you leave out?
check.why: Never type bank or card numbers into an AI tool.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Treating customers well
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write clear, polite messages and handle a problem with a customer.
This lesson builds toward: With each customer, you will confirm each job's details in a polite message and respond to problems, telling your parent or guardian about anything unsafe or unpaid.
Customers come back, and tell friends, when you are on time, polite and honest. Confirm each job: day, time, price and what you will do.
AI can help you write messages, with your parent or guardian copied on them: "Write a polite message confirming a dog walk on Saturday at 10 am for the agreed price." If something goes wrong, say sorry, explain what you will do to fix it, and keep your promise.
If a customer is rude, asks you to do something unsafe or does not pay, stop and tell your parent or guardian. You do not have to handle it alone.
Step by step:
- Confirm day, time, price and task before every job.
- Be on time and do what you promised.
- If something goes wrong: say sorry, say your fix, do it.
- Unsafe or unpaid? Tell your parent or guardian.
Words to know:
- Confirm: check and agree on details before the job.
- Review: what a customer says about your work.
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page side hustle plan: service and customer, price and why, your flyer, your money tracker, and two safety rules. Show it to a parent or guardian and ask what they would change.
You can now plan and run a small, safe side hustle with AI as your helper.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Service and customer The service or the customer is unclear. Says what the service is, who it is for, and that at least three people said they would pay. Also shows the idea fits the learner's real weekly hours. Price No price, or no reason for it. One clear price that covers costs and time, checked with local people. Shows the cost per job and how the price compares to local options. Flyer The flyer has a home address, or no price or contact. A headline, short points, the price and an approved contact, with no home address. The words were edited to sound like the learner, and the design is easy to read. Money tracker Missing columns or no way to see profit. Date, money in, money out and notes, with a total that shows profit. Has real or practice entries and a note on when it will be checked each week. Safety rules Fewer than two safety rules, or no parent or guardian review. Two safety rules agreed with a parent or guardian, who has seen the plan. Also notes the youth work and tax rules that apply, checked on official sites. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What should a job confirmation message include?
options: The day, time, price and task
check.why: Confirming the day, time, price and task avoids mix-ups.

check.q: You forgot to refill a pet's water bowl. What do you do?
options: Say sorry, explain your fix and do it
check.why: Owning the mistake and fixing it keeps customers' trust.
